summary: Describes a structure for representing trust anchor information. A trust anchor is an authoritative entity represented by a public key plus data that limits what it is trusted for. It meets the format needs set out in the trust anchor management requirements. It is a Proposed Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: A list of the people you trust the most, written down in a standard form, with notes on what each one is trusted to do.

questions: what is a trust anchor list
subtitle: A standard, compact record of a trust anchor: its public key plus limits on what it is trusted to vouch for.

tldr.problem: Trust anchors are needed to validate certification paths, but there was no standard format for representing trust anchor information.
tldr.mechanism: The TrustAnchorInfo structure, written in ASN.1, holds the public key, a key identifier, an optional title and optional certification path controls. A TrustAnchorList can hold many anchors.
tldr.outcome: Trust anchors can be exchanged in a compact form, and constraints can be attached without breaking a certificate's signature. The RFC is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 5914 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2010. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why a Trust Anchor Format
sections.content:
A trust anchor is an authoritative entity represented by a public key and associated data. The key verifies digital signatures, and the associated data limits the types of information or actions for which the anchor is authoritative. Trust anchors are required when validating certification paths.

Although they are widely used, there was no standard format for trust anchor information. RFC 5914 defines the TrustAnchorInfo structure in ASN.1 to fill that gap and to meet the format requirements of the trust anchor management requirements document. It can be a more compact alternative to X.509 certificates, and it can attach extra or alternative constraints without breaking the signature on a certificate.
sections.plainLanguage: Grown-ups need a clear way to say 'I trust this one, for these jobs only.' This RFC gives everyone the same note-card layout for that.

sections.title: The TrustAnchorInfo Structure
sections.content:
TrustAnchorInfo is an ASN.1 SEQUENCE with seven fields. Only the public key and key identifier are always present.

  • version: defaults to v1, and that default cannot be changed by later updates. Future changes should increment the number.
  • pubKey: a SubjectPublicKeyInfo holding the algorithm identifier and the public key, encoded as a BIT STRING.
  • keyId: the key identifier of the anchor's public key, calculated by the common methods in RFC 5280.
  • taTitle: optional human-readable name, 1 to 64 UTF-8 characters.
  • certPath: optional certification path controls.
  • exts: optional extensions.
  • taTitleLangTag: optional language of the title. When absent, English (en) is used.
sections.plainLanguage: The note card has a spot for the key, a name tag for the key, and some optional extras like a friendly title and rules about what the key may be trusted for.

sections.title: Certification Path Controls
sections.content:
The optional CertPathControls supply the starting inputs for X.509 certification path validation. When it is absent, the trust anchor cannot be used to validate the signature on an X.509 certificate. It holds:

  • taName: the X.500 distinguished name of the anchor. It MUST NOT be an empty sequence.
  • certificate: an optional X.509 certificate. If present, its subject name MUST exactly match taName, its public key MUST match pubKey, and any subject key identifier extension MUST match keyId.
  • policySet: certificate policy identifiers fed to the validation algorithm. When absent, any-policy is used. Policy qualifiers MUST NOT be included.
  • policyFlags: three Booleans, inhibitPolicyMapping, requireExplicitPolicy and inhibitAnyPolicy. When absent they are all FALSE, the most liberal setting.
  • nameConstr: permitted and excluded name subtrees for later certificates. When absent, permitted names are unbounded and excluded names are empty.
  • pathLenConstraint: the maximum number of non-self-issued intermediate certificates that may follow. Zero means none may follow. When absent, there is no limit.

An application validating a path SHOULD NOT ignore these limits, but it MAY tighten them, for example by supplying a subset of the policies or permitted names, extra excluded names, or a smaller path length.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like a permission slip for a class trip: it says which doors the key may open and how many helpers can pass the trust along. A teacher may add rules, but may not skip them.

sections.title: Working With Certificates and Extensions
sections.content:
If a certificate is wrapped inside TrustAnchorInfo, the constraints in policySet, policyFlags, nameConstr, pathLenConstraint and exts replace the values in the certificate or supply values for extensions it lacks. Values in the TrustAnchorInfo fields are always enforced. Extensions in the certificate are enforced only when there is no corresponding TrustAnchorInfo value.

The RFC maps each certificate extension to its counterpart. For example, the certificate policies extension corresponds to policySet, and the name constraints extension corresponds to nameConstr. Any other extension corresponds to the same type in exts. Four extension types (certificate policies, policy constraints, inhibit any policy and name constraints) MUST NOT appear in exts and are ignored if they do, to avoid duplication.
sections.plainLanguage: If an old ID card and the new note card disagree, the note card wins, so the rules on it always count.

sections.title: The Trust Anchor List
sections.content:
A single TrustAnchorInfo describes one anchor. For collections, TrustAnchorList is a sequence of one or more TrustAnchorChoice objects. Each choice is one of three options:

  • certificate: a plain certificate with no added constraints.
  • tbsCert: a certificate with its signature removed and its extensions changed, which lets constraints be attached.
  • taInfo: a TrustAnchorInfo structure.

A list can be protected with the CMS SignedData structure from RFC 5652. The object identifier id-ct-trustAnchorList identifies list payloads in CMS.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of one card you can keep a whole stack. Each card can be a plain ID, an ID with the signature peeled off, or the special note card.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
If a trust anchor private key is compromised, unauthorized parties can masquerade as the anchor, with potentially severe consequences. Where trust-anchor constraints are enforced, the attacker is limited by the certification path controls. For example, name constraints determine the name space accepted for certificates validated with the compromised anchor. Relying on an incorrect trust anchor public key has similar consequences.

A compromised CA private key causes the same kind of problems and is limited by the same controls. Using a certificate independently of the TrustAnchorInfo that wraps it must be carefully managed so the constraints are not violated, and values in the certificate should be checked for conflicts with the wrapper.
sections.plainLanguage: If a thief steals a trusted key, the rules on the card still limit what they can do, but it is still very bad, so keep keys safe.
